title: DHS Domestic Terrorism Warning Suppression - Ignoring White Supremacist Threat
description_short: DHS Domestic Terrorism Warning Suppression - Ignoring White Supremacist Threat
description_medium: An August 2020 Everytown post summarized Politico reporting that White House officials did not want to discuss rising domestic-extremist threats or use the term “domestic terrorism.” Former DHS official Elizabeth Neumann described a growing white-supremacist danger, while a state law-enforcement official said DHS intelligence products disproportionately emphasized left-wing extremism. The account also reported frustration and departures among department officials.
description_long: Everytown’s August 2020 post summarized Politico reporting that Department of Homeland Security employees were warning about white-supremacist domestic terrorism. It quoted former assistant secretary Elizabeth Neumann’s warning that a globalized white-supremacist threat was materializing, while she believed the government was doing too little about domestic extremists. According to the report, White House officials did not want to discuss the rising threat or use the phrase “domestic terrorism.” The post also relayed an unnamed state law-enforcement official’s assessment that DHS intelligence sent to state and local partners gave disproportionate emphasis to left-wing extremism. Separately, it cited a Center for Strategic and International Studies review estimating that right-wing extremists were responsible for nearly two-thirds of U.S. terror attacks and plots in 2019 and more than 90 percent from January through early May 2020. These details frame the reported gap between threat warnings and attention. The account does not demonstrate that every intelligence product was altered by White House direction or establish a causal connection between the reported suppression and specific attacks, so this description focuses on what its sources reported.

title: Pardons Thomas K. Ford
description_short: Trump granted a presidential pardon to Thomas K. Ford as part of a clemency list.
description_medium: The Justice Department’s pardon register lists Thomas K. Ford among Trump’s January 13, 2021 grants and identifies a Southern District of Illinois case. It records a 2003 sentence of three years’ probation and a $2,000 fine for violating mandatory safety standards and making false material statements. The listing confirms a pardon but gives no reason for it.
description_long: The Justice Department’s register places Thomas K. Ford among Donald Trump’s January 13, 2021 pardons. It identifies Ford’s case in the Southern District of Illinois and lists a sentence imposed on April 10, 2003: three years of probation and a $2,000 fine. The listed offenses were violating mandatory safety standards and making false material statements and representations. This public entry supplies the basic legal context for the pardon, but it does not describe the underlying incident, explain what Ford did, or state why Trump selected him for clemency. A presidential pardon is a form of relief from federal consequences; the register confirms the grant without documenting a political connection, private benefit, or improper exchange. Those limits matter because the record’s “Corrupt Pardons” subcategory should not be treated as evidence of corruption on its own. The DOJ entry supports a factual account of who received a pardon and the original sentence, while the pardon warrant or another case-specific source would be needed to establish the circumstances or rationale behind it.
